# CREED: everything in one file

> CREED is the Wayne State app stack's code book: a handbook of numbered practices, plus policy.json, one file of support dates for PHP, Laravel, Node, MySQL, Vue and Inertia, and a small PHP reader every other tool asks: what state is this version in, on this date?

The README and the Markdown twin of every page, joined. The index is https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/llms.txt. Written by Squire's agent-ready kit; do not edit.

---

## README

Source: https://github.com/waynestate/creed/blob/HEAD/README.md

## CREED

**The standard everything rests on.** The Wayne State App Stack Code: one policy file, one reader, and an
inspector who stamps what he finds.

Checks: `composer ci` (the same command runs on GitLab and GitHub).

Front page: [`site/index.html`](https://github.com/waynestate/creed/blob/HEAD/site/index.html), a static page you can open in a browser or serve from `site/`.
On Citadel it is served by the raw-PHP deploy layer in [`deploy/`](https://github.com/waynestate/creed/blob/HEAD/deploy/): a Squire kit whose front controller serves `site/` behind HELMET's security headers. For local development, keep serving `site/` directly.

One command, two clouds, zero excuses. Higher.

CREED is the Wayne State app stack's version policy, as data. One file,
`policy/policy.json`, lists the support dates for PHP, Laravel, Node, MySQL,
Vue and Inertia, plus the rules every check runs against. A small
framework-free PHP reader, `Waynestate\Creed\Policy`, answers the one question
every tool needs: what state is this version in, on this date?

This repository is published from Wayne State University's internal GitLab
and mirrored here. Changes land there first; Wayne State developers open
issues and merge requests on the internal project.

No other code in the stack decides a version's state. The rules live in one
place, and every tool reads them from here.

### Install

```
composer require waynestate/creed
```

### Usage

```php
use Waynestate\Creed\Policy;
use Waynestate\Creed\State;

$policy = Policy::bundled();

// What state is PHP 8.2 in, on this date?
$state = $policy->stateOf('php', '8.2', new DateTimeImmutable('2026-10-27'));
// State::Security

// What is the oldest PHP an app may declare?
$floor = $policy->oldestSupported('php', new DateTimeImmutable('2026-10-27'));
// '8.2'
```

#### Reading the policy from PHP

The reader's public members, one line each:

- `Policy::bundled()`, `Policy::fromFile($path)`, `Policy::fromArray($data)`: load a policy; `origin()` says where it came from.
- `stateOf($component, $version, $on)`: the state, or an exception; `tryStateOf()` is the same answer as `null` when it cannot be answered.
- `oldestSupported($component, $on)`: the lowest version still Active or Security; `supported()` lists all of them, oldest first.
- `latestPatch($component, $version)`: the current patch in that line; `latestPatchChecked()` says when it was last checked.
- `line($component, $version)`: the raw line, with `active_until`, `security_until`, `latest_patch`, `latest_patch_checked` (each a string or null) and `current` (true or null).
- `activeUntil()`, `securityUntil()`: those dates as `DateTimeImmutable`, or null.
- `daysToEol($component, $version, $on)`: whole days until `security_until`, signed; `isPastGrace()` says whether the grace period is over.
- `resolveVersion($component, $version)`: the policy line a full version like `8.3.12` belongs to.
- `isAheadOfPolicy($component, $version)`: whether a version sorts above every line the policy lists.
- `belowOldestLineReason($component, $version)`: the reason a version is `Eol` for sorting below every listed line, or null.
- `hasComponent()`, `components()`, `versions($component)`, `tools()`, `toolMinimum($tool)`, `rules()`: the shape of the policy itself.

One last time: the reader answers, it does not guess.

#### With Arms Wide Open

The support window stays open until `security_until`. A version is still
`Security` on that day, moves to `Eol` the day after, and stays in `Eol` for
`eol_grace_days` (90) more days before it is `EolGraceExpired`. The boundary
is inclusive, and the reader never guesses.

#### Versions CREED hasn't heard of

The reader refuses what it does not know, except the newest thing and the
oldest. A version that sorts above every line the policy lists is `Active`,
and `isAheadOfPolicy()` says so. A version that parses and sorts below every
listed line is `Eol`: it is older than the oldest listed line, and that is
end of life by definition. `belowOldestLineReason()` gives the reason,
`older than the oldest listed line (8.1)`. A version that falls between
listed lines, or that does not parse, is still unknown, and still throws.
Current versions are never refused.

A line marked `"current": true` is `Active` on every date and carries no
`security_until`: the policy says the line is current, and the reader does not
guess when it stops being so.

#### Higher

CREED itself requires PHP `^8.3`, like every stack package, and CI tests it on
8.3, 8.4 and 8.5. The policy's floor for apps is a different number: `^8.2`
until PHP 8.2 reaches end of life on 2026-12-31, then `^8.3`. Creed has always
been one version ahead of everyone else, at least by his own account.

### Proof

Proof runs against real Wayne State applications are on a private
site, [proof.apps.wayne.edu/creed](https://proof.apps.wayne.edu/creed/), behind a Wayne State employee sign-in.

### The handbook

The rules, chapter by chapter, live in [`handbook/`](https://github.com/waynestate/creed/blob/HEAD/handbook/README.md).

### Keeping the patches fresh

`bin/refresh-patches.php` re-reads the upstream feeds, rewrites the
`latest_patch` fields in `policy/policy.json`, and proposes new Vue lines from
endoflife.date. A scheduled CI job runs it every
Monday and fails the pipeline when the policy is stale; a person then runs the
tool and commits the result. CI never pushes. It only raises its hand.

The schedule is a GitLab project setting, not a file in this repo: someone
creates it under CI/CD > Schedules (weekly, Monday). The GitHub mirror runs the
same check on a cron and on demand.

### Refreshing the policy

`bin/refresh-policy.php` keeps every support date, patch and new line in
`policy/policy.json` tied to a canonical source, so nobody types a date by
hand. PHP dates come from php.net, Node dates from the Node.js release
schedule, and Laravel, MySQL, Vue and Composer from endoflife.date; patches
come from php.net, nodejs.org, Packagist and npm. Each run sorts every change:

| Class | What it is | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| `tighten` | a date moves earlier, or a `current` line gets its first end date | written |
| `neutral` | a new `latest_patch`, or a new line above every listed line | written |
| `loosen-warning` | `active_until` moves later (a warning tier, never a failure) | written |
| `loosen-fail` | `security_until` moves later, or an EOL line would be supported again | held, unless two independent sources agree (php.net and endoflife.date for PHP, schedule.json and endoflife.date for Node) or `policy/sources.json` shows the same value from the same source for 14 days |
| `refused` | removing a line or a date, or any change to `tools` or `rules` | never automatic; reported (a Composer minimum on an EOL line shows up here) |

A source that is down, slow or returns something unreadable changes nothing:
its fields keep their last good value. A line missing from a feed is never
removed. Where a first-party source and endoflife.date disagree, the first
party wins and the disagreement is reported.

```
php bin/refresh-policy.php [--dry-run] [--offline <dir>] [--policy <path>]
    [--sources <path>] [--report <file>] [--today YYYY-MM-DD] [--touch]
```

`--report` writes JSON with `changes`, `held`, `refused`,
`disagreements` and `source_errors`. `--touch` sets `refreshed_on` to today even
when nothing else changed (the weekly heartbeat). `policy/sources.json` records,
per value, which source said it, and the first and last day it was seen.

Exit codes: `0` nothing worth committing (always `0` with `--dry-run`); `1` hard
failure; `3` something was written to `policy/policy.json` or `policy/sources.json`,
including a released `loosen-fail` (the policy robot raises the alert from the
report); `4` something was held or refused; nothing is committed for that run.
Written changes are always written.
`bin/refresh-patches.php` still works as before.

### Carrying CREED in another package

PROCTOR, Booster and Rollcall each carry a generated copy of the reader
under their own namespace, so two tools in one app never fight over a class
name (the generator below keeps the copies in step). ADVISOR carries CREED's
policy and handbook as a data bundle instead. The copies began
because CREED was not on Packagist. It is now (`waynestate/creed` 0.1.3), so
each copy can become a real `require`, one consumer at a time; until a
consumer switches, its copy stays. CREED owns the generator and the check:

```
php bin/export.php --namespace=Waynestate\Proctor\Creed --to=vendor/creed-copy
php bin/export.php --check --namespace=Waynestate\Proctor\Creed --to=vendor/creed-copy
```

The copy is the reader with the namespace rewritten and `bundled()` repointed
at its own `policy.json`; `--check` fails when the copy drifts from the source.
Creed Bratton would have a form for this.

### Tests

Maintainers: how to build, test and release this project, and where its data comes from, is in [MAINTAINING.md](https://github.com/waynestate/creed/blob/HEAD/MAINTAINING.md).

No PHP on the machine? Fine. Docker runs the suite:

```
docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/app" -w /app composer:2 composer install --no-interaction
docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/app" -w /app php:8.4-cli vendor/bin/phpunit
docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/app" -w /app php:8.3-cli vendor/bin/phpunit
```

The policy validates against its schema:

```
docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/app" -w /app composer:2 composer validate-policy
```

### Strongly recommended: a git.wayne.edu instance runner

git.wayne.edu has no runners today. Every product in the stack strongly
recommends a git.wayne.edu instance runner.

Creed Bratton, whose quality assurance work we all admire. His past is a
mystery. Ours is in `policy/policy.json`, where it belongs.

---

Wayne State App Stack 2026 Edition Adopted 2026-10-29

## CREED The Wayne State App Stack Code

§0.1 Short title

This code shall be known as CREED, which stands for

C&IT Rules for Every Enterprise Developer

and may be cited as *the standard everything rests on*.

The written development standards for Wayne State's app stack: a handbook of numbered practices, plus `policy.json`, one file of support dates for PHP, Laravel, Node, MySQL, Vue and Inertia. A small PHP reader answers the one question every other tool asks: *what state is this version in, on this date?*

**Already included in [WELD](https://weld.apps.wayne.edu/).** Use CREED on its own when an app or tool that isn't WELD needs the stack's rules, or the support dates in `policy.json`.

[Inspect a version](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/#inspection) [Read the handbook](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/)

- **Enforced**: 5
- **Checked**: 7
- **Documented**: 14
- **Not yet**: 28

Table of contents

### Ten chapters, 54 practices

Each practice has a reason, sources and a stamp that says how the stack holds it today. Clause numbers follow the chapters: §2.1 is practice 11 in [BEST_PRACTICES.md](https://github.com/waynestate/creed/blob/main/BEST_PRACTICES.md). This page prints the clauses an inspector reaches for most; the book has all of them, and the rules themselves are in [the handbook](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/), chapter by chapter.

1. [1 The version policy as data §1.1 to §1.10](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/#ch-1)
2. [2 PHP and framework versions §2.1 to §2.7](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/#ch-2)
3. [3 Dependencies §3.1 to §3.6](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/#ch-3)
4. [4 Secrets and configuration §4.1 to §4.3](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/#ch-4)
5. [5 Overrides and rollout §5.1 to §5.3](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/#ch-5)
6. [6 Writing the handbook §6.1 to §6.7](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/#ch-6)
7. [7 Patching and the supply chain §7.1 to §7.9](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/#ch-7)
8. [8 Platform and database §8.1 to §8.3](https://github.com/waynestate/creed/blob/main/BEST_PRACTICES.md#8-platform-and-database-second-pass)
9. [9 Policy data §9.1 to §9.3](https://github.com/waynestate/creed/blob/main/BEST_PRACTICES.md#9-policy-data-second-pass)
10. [10 Accessibility and the legal floor §10.1 to §10.3](https://github.com/waynestate/creed/blob/main/BEST_PRACTICES.md#10-accessibility-and-the-legal-floor-second-pass)

#### Key to the stamps

- **Enforced**: Code makes the violation impossible, or a test fails CI.
- **Checked**: PROCTOR or CI warns or fails. The check is named.
- **Documented**: Written down only.
- **Not yet**: A gap. Printed anyway, because an honest gap beats a quiet one.

Art. I

#### The policy

`policy/policy.json` holds every support date as an ISO day, plus the rules: an audit threshold of `high`, banned constraints `dev-*` and `*`, and a grace of 90 days. A schema guards it.

Art. II

#### The reader

`Waynestate\Creed\Policy`, framework-free PHP. `stateOf` returns `Active`, `Security`, `Eol` or `EolGraceExpired`. No other code in the stack decides a version's state.

Art. III

#### The handbook

The rules chapter by chapter in [the handbook](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/), each citing the decision behind it. Where nothing is decided, the chapter says "To be decided" and states no rule.

Form CR-1 · Field inspection

### Inspect a version

Pick a runtime, a version and a day. The inspector reads the same dates as `Policy::stateOf`, by the same rules: the end day is inclusive, then 90 days of grace, then nothing. He stamps what he finds.

Certificate of inspection

No. 0001

- **Runtime**: PHP 8.2
- **Inspected on**: 2026-10-29
- **Reader call**: `$policy->stateOf('php', '8.2', new DateTimeImmutable('2026-10-29'))`
- **Returns**: `State::Security`

Security fixes only, until 2026-12-31: 63 days left. Plan the move to PHP 8.4 now.

Applicable clause: [§2.2 Treat security-only as a countdown, not a resting place](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/#c-2-2)

Inspector CREED reader, schema v1

Chapter 1

### The version policy as data

Creed Bratton keeps his own records and nobody can audit them. CREED does the opposite: every date is in one file, with a source, where anyone can check it.

#### §1.1 Keep one machine-readable policy, and let one reader decide state.

Every tool reads `policy.json` through the CREED reader. No other code decides whether a version is active, security-only or EOL.

Held by `Waynestate\Creed\Policy`, the only implementation. [PROCTOR](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/#ahj-proctor) is meant to depend on it.

Documented

**Rationale.** Two tools with two copies of a date will eventually disagree, and a developer cannot tell which to believe.

#### §1.2 Validate the policy file against a schema in CI.

A bad date, a wrong type or an unknown key fails the build.

Held by `PolicySchemaTest` and `composer validate-policy`, both in [Preflight](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/#ahj-preflight) `php-test`.

Enforced

**Rationale.** A typo in a date silently changes what every tool reports.

#### §1.4 Make the reader refuse to guess.

A version with no `security_until` is an error, not a silent pass, unless its line is marked current. An unknown component, or a version between the listed lines, is an error. A version older than the oldest listed line is EOL. A version newer than every listed line is Active: current versions are never refused.

Held by `stateOf`, which throws for each error case, and `isAheadOfPolicy`; tests cover every one.

Enforced

**Rationale.** A tool that guesses turns missing data into a green check.

#### §1.5 Compute state from the date, with an inclusive end and a stated grace period.

A version is still supported on its `security_until` day. It is EOL the next day. After `eol_grace_days` (90) it is past grace, and no override applies.

Held by `PolicyStateTest`, on the PHP 8.2 boundary days.

Enforced

**Rationale.** Everyone must get the same answer on the same day, including on the boundary. *With arms wide open*: the window stays open through the last day.

#### §1.9 Model support honestly when a project publishes no dates.

Vue 3 and Inertia publish no fixed end dates. Do not invent them. The policy marks Vue 3, Inertia 2 and Inertia 3 `"current": true`: Active on every date, with no `security_until`. Vue 2 keeps its real end, 2023-12-31.

Held by the schema, which refuses a current line that carries `security_until` and a dated line without it; `PolicySchemaTest` covers both.

Enforced

**Rationale.** A made-up date is worse than an honest "no date".

Chapter 2

### PHP and framework versions

EOL PHP is not supported by the stack, with no exceptions. The adopted editions are in Table 2-1.

#### §2.1 Run non-EOL PHP only.

Apps declare and run a PHP version that php.net lists as supported. On 2026-10-29 that means 8.2 (security only, to 2026-12-31), 8.3, 8.4 and 8.5.

Held by [PROCTOR](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/#ahj-proctor) `php-floor`, which fails when the lowest bound of `require.php` is EOL by policy.

Checked

**Rationale.** An EOL branch receives no security fixes.

#### §2.2 Treat security-only as a countdown, not a resting place.

A version in security-only support warns now and fails on the day after `security_until`. Plan the move before then.

Held by [PROCTOR](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/#ahj-proctor) `php-floor` (a WARN). [HELMET](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/#ahj-helmet) ships the runtime ribbon.

Checked

**Rationale.** Moving on a deadline day is how upgrades go wrong.

#### §2.3 Raise the floor on the day the old version ends.

The PHP floor for apps moves from `^8.2` to `^8.3` on 2027-01-01. CREED itself already requires `^8.3`; Creed has always been one version ahead of everyone else, at least by his own account.

Held by `oldestSupported` computes it. No automation bumps a package's constraint.

Documented

**Rationale.** It is the only way a dependency floor can force an upgrade.

Table 2-1 Adopted editions, with the state on 2026-10-29

| Runtime | Active until | Security until | Latest patch | State |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PHP floor **8.2** |  |  |  |  |
| 8.5 | 2027-12-31 | 2029-12-31 | 8.5.12 | Active |
| 8.4 | 2026-12-31 | 2028-12-31 | 8.4.27 | Active |
| 8.3 | 2025-12-31 | 2027-12-31 | 8.3.36 | Security |
| 8.2 | 2024-12-31 | 2026-12-31 | 8.2.35 | Security |
| 8.1 | 2023-11-25 | 2025-12-31 | n/a | Grace expired |
| Laravel floor **12** |  |  |  |  |
| 13 | 2027-09-30 | 2028-03-17 | 13.39.0 | Active |
| 12 | 2026-08-13 | 2027-02-24 | 12.70.2 | Security |
| 11 | 2025-09-03 | 2026-03-12 | 11.57.1 | Grace expired |
| 10 | 2024-08-06 | 2025-02-04 | 10.50.4 | Grace expired |
| Node floor **22** |  |  |  |  |
| 26 | 2027-10-20 | 2029-04-30 | 26.13.0 | Active |
| 24 | 2026-10-20 | 2028-04-30 | 24.22.2 | Security |
| 22 | 2025-10-21 | 2027-04-30 | 22.23.4 | Security |
| 20 | 2024-10-22 | 2026-04-30 | 20.20.2 | Grace expired |
| MySQL floor **8.4** |  |  |  |  |
| 9.7 | 2031-04-30 | 2034-04-30 | n/a | Active |
| 8.4 | 2029-04-30 | 2032-04-30 | n/a | Active |
| 8.0 | 2025-04-30 | 2026-04-30 | n/a | Grace expired |
| 5.7 | 2020-10-31 | 2023-10-31 | n/a | Grace expired |
| 5.6 | 2018-02-28 | 2021-02-28 | n/a | Grace expired |
| Vue and Inertia |  |  |  |  |
| Vue 2 | 2023-12-31 | 2023-12-31 | n/a | Grace expired |
| Vue 3 | Current line: no published end dates, none invented; see §1.9. | Active |  |  |
| Inertia 2 | Current line: no published end dates, none invented; see §1.9. | Active |  |  |
| Inertia 3 | Current line: no published end dates, none invented; see §1.9. | Active |  |  |

From `policy/policy.json`, schema version 1, patches checked 2026-10-28 and 2026-10-29. For Node, "active" holds the maintenance start; for MySQL, the Premier end. That mapping is the policy's, not the vendors' wording.

#### §2.5 Run a Laravel release that still gets security fixes.

Laravel gives bug fixes for 18 months and security fixes for two years. Laravel 11 and older are EOL. Laravel 12 gets security fixes until 2027-02-24; Laravel 13 until 2028-03-17.

Gap The reader can classify 10 to 13. PROCTOR `unpatched` reads `laravel/framework` from `composer.lock` and warns when the locked patch trails the policy's `latest_patch`, but no check fails an app whose framework line is EOL; the planned deploy gate will.

Not yet

**Rationale.** An EOL framework is the largest unpatched surface in a typical app.

#### §2.6 Use a Node release that is in LTS or maintenance.

Build front ends on a Node line that has not reached end of life: 22, 24 and 26. Node 20 reached end of life on 2026-04-30.

Gap The dates are in `policy.json`; no check reads an app's Node version yet.

Not yet

**Rationale.** Build tools run with your credentials and your source.

#### §2.7 Choose a supported MySQL, and say when the platform lags.

MySQL 8.4 LTS has Premier support to 2029-04-30 and Extended to 2032-04-30. MySQL 8.0 ended on 2026-04-30 and is past CREED's 90-day grace since 2026-07-29.

Gap Nothing checks it, and the platform's own MySQL timeline is still an open question.

Not yet

**Rationale.** A database that no longer gets fixes holds everything above it back.

Chapter 3

### Dependencies

What goes into an app, and how it is allowed in.

#### §3.1 Commit the lock file.

`composer.lock` is in the repository for apps. Use `composer install` in CI and on deploy, not `composer update`.

Held by [PROCTOR](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/#ahj-proctor) `lock-committed`.

Checked

**Rationale.** Without a lock, a build next week is a different build.

#### §3.2 Ban open-ended constraints.

No `dev-*` branches and no `*` on runtime dependencies. Use caret constraints such as `^2.4`.

Held by [PROCTOR](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/#ahj-proctor) `unbounded-constraints`, using `banned_constraints` from the policy.

Checked

**Rationale.** An open constraint lets an unreviewed change into production.

#### §3.3 Audit dependencies and fail at a stated severity.

Run `composer audit --locked` in CI and fail at or above the policy threshold, `high`.

Held by [Preflight](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/#ahj-preflight) `composer-audit` and [PROCTOR](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/#ahj-proctor) `composer-audit`.

Checked

**Rationale.** Known advisories are the cheapest attacks to run.

#### §3.6 Pin CI components to a tag or SHA.

Include shared CI components at a tag or a full commit SHA, never `~latest`. CREED's own pipeline pins both of its components to a SHA.

Held by `ci.md`; components from [Preflight](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/#ahj-preflight). No check scans other repos.

Documented

**Rationale.** A moving reference lets an upstream change weaken your pipeline without a commit in your repo.

Chapter 4

### Secrets and configuration

Three practices, three gaps, all printed. The inspector would rather you knew.

#### §4.1 Keep secrets out of source control.

Do not commit `.env`, keys, tokens or passwords. Commit `.env.example` with placeholders. Rotate a secret that was ever exposed.

Gap No handbook chapter covers secrets, and no check scans for them yet.

Not yet

**Rationale.** A repository is copied to many machines and outlives any one password.

#### §4.3 Never run production with debug on.

`APP_DEBUG` is `false` in production.

Gap The runtime and headers chapter says "To be decided"; [HELMET](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/#ahj-helmet)'s refusal rules are not built.

Not yet

**Rationale.** Debug pages expose configuration values to users.

Chapter 5

### Overrides and rollout

Every code has variances. These are the rules for asking for one.

#### §5.1 Make every exception named, dated and visible.

An override sits in the app's `policy-overrides.json` with a reason and an expiry. Every run prints every override. An expired override fails.

Held by [PROCTOR](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/#ahj-proctor) `overrides`. [Rollcall](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/#ahj-rollcall) counts expired overrides across apps in its fleet report.

Checked

**Rationale.** An exception without an end date becomes the rule.

#### §5.2 Roll a new rule out in stages, with dates.

Each rule moves `report`, then `warn`, then `block`. A deploy that does not make things worse always passes.

Held by the proposed deploy gate. The schema has no field for stage dates yet.

Documented

**Rationale.** Blocking every non-compliant app on day one blocks the fixes too.

Chapter 6

### Writing the handbook

How the code itself is kept: decisions cited, questions owned, checks that give the same answer twice.

#### §6.1 Cite the decision behind every rule.

Each handbook rule links to the ADR that decided it. Where nothing is decided, the chapter says "To be decided" and states no rule.

Documented

**Rationale.** Readers can trust a rule, and can find who to ask about the rest.

#### §6.4 Judge with deterministic checks only.

No gate depends on a language model's opinion. A model may explain a failure; it does not decide pass or fail.

Documented

**Rationale.** A gate must give the same answer twice.

#### §6.5 Keep every developer tool usable on Windows, macOS and Linux.

Scripts ship as a `.ps1` and `.sh` pair, or as one PHP command. Every repo carries `.gitattributes` with `* text=auto eol=lf`.

Documented

**Rationale.** Developers work on all three, and the servers need LF.

#### §6.6 Run the test suite on every supported PHP version.

CI runs CREED's unit tests on 8.3, 8.4 and 8.5, from its own floor up.

Held by [Preflight](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/#ahj-preflight) `php-test`, a matrix in CREED's pipeline.

Checked

**Rationale.** A library that works only on the newest PHP excludes half its users.

Chapter 7 · Added in the second pass

### Patching and the supply chain

Nine practices, one held so far. Chapters 8 to 10 (platform and database, policy data, accessibility) are all "Not yet" and are in the book.

#### §7.1 Track the PHP patch release, not only the branch.

A supported branch is not a patched one. On 2026-10-21 PHP released 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 to fix two critical advisories. `policy.json` now carries a `latest_patch` for each branch.

Held by `latestPatch()` in the reader; maintainers refresh it with `php bin/refresh-patches.php`.

Documented

**Rationale.** The branch tells you whether fixes still come; the patch tells you whether you took them.

Inserted after printing

### Errata and pending amendments

Open questions in the 2026 edition. Each is written down with the clause it touches, and stays open until a decision or a source closes it.

| No. | Clause | Erratum or amendment | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| E-4 | §9.3 | Strict or tolerant schema: can an older tool still read a newer policy that only added a field? A test with an old schema and reader decides. | Open |
| E-5 | §9.1 | Node 27 and later have no Maintenance phase on the new yearly schedule, so how `active_until` is derived needs a new rule. | Open |
| E-6 | Ch. 10 | The accessibility chapter: aim at WCAG 2.2 AA, after confirming which legal dates apply. To be decided. | Open |
| E-7 | Handbook | Runtime and headers: no rules until a decision lands with HELMET. The auth chapter still has the gateway's key distribution, and the SAML library if a SAML driver is built, to decide. | Open |

The full backlog, 37 items, is at the end of [BEST_PRACTICES.md](https://github.com/waynestate/creed/blob/main/BEST_PRACTICES.md#gaps-for-the-backlog).

Referenced tools

CREED writes the rules; the rest of WELD inspects, builds and runs to them. Every tool below reads `policy.json` through the reader, never through its own copy.

Appendix A

### Adopting this code

Read the policy from your tool, or run CREED's own checks in a clone.

#### A.1 Read the policy from PHP

Any OS with PHP 8.3 or newer and Composer. On Packagist, 0.1.3

`$ composer require waynestate/creed`

```
use Waynestate\Creed\Policy;
use Waynestate\Creed\State;

$policy = Policy::bundled();

// What state is PHP 8.2 in, on this date?
$state = $policy->stateOf('php', '8.2', new DateTimeImmutable('2026-10-27'));
// State::Security

// What is the oldest PHP an app may declare?
$floor = $policy->oldestSupported('php', new DateTimeImmutable('2026-10-27'));
// '8.2'
```

#### A.2 Run CREED's checks

In a clone, with PHP and Composer installed, one command runs the whole gate (validate, PHPUnit, policy schema, Pint, PHPStan, audit). The same command runs on GitLab and GitHub.

`$ composer ci`

No PHP on the machine? Docker runs the suite and the schema check.

**Windows**

PowerShell, with Docker Desktop.

```
PS> docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/app" -w /app composer:2 composer install --no-interaction
PS> docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/app" -w /app php:8.4-cli vendor/bin/phpunit
PS> docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/app" -w /app composer:2 composer validate-policy
```

**macOS**

Terminal, with Docker Desktop.

```
$ docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/app" -w /app composer:2 composer install --no-interaction
$ docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/app" -w /app php:8.4-cli vendor/bin/phpunit
$ docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/app" -w /app composer:2 composer validate-policy
```

**Linux**

Any shell, with Docker Engine.

```
$ docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/app" -w /app composer:2 composer install --no-interaction
$ docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/app" -w /app php:8.4-cli vendor/bin/phpunit
$ docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/app" -w /app composer:2 composer validate-policy
```

Maintainers refresh the patch numbers from the upstream feeds with `php bin/refresh-patches.php --dry-run` (drop `--dry-run` to write).

**Strongly recommended:** a git.wayne.edu instance runner. CI is a gate only if something runs it (§6.7), and git.wayne.edu has no runners today.

Appendix B

### Hand it to your agent

Four forms, ready to file with the coding agent you already use. Copy one, or run it straight in OpenCode, Claude Code, Codex or ChatGPT. Each one tells the agent where the code lives, what it may not assume, and to ask before it guesses.

#### Get started with CREED

What CREED says about every version your app runs, today, and the smallest change that brings it back up to code.

A prompt for your coding agent. Copy it as it stands:

```text
You are a coding agent helping a Wayne State University developer bring the app in this folder up to CREED, the written standard of WELD, the Wayne State application stack. CREED is two things: policy.json, the support dates for PHP, Laravel, Node, MySQL, Vue and Inertia, and a handbook of numbered practices.

Read first:
- https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/llms.txt, the index of CREED's pages, each one as Markdown. Fetch the pages you need; do not work from memory.
- This app's composer.json and composer.lock, and package.json with its lock file if there is one.
- ADVISOR, the stack's MCP server, if it is connected: its policy_lookup and list_stack_rules tools answer from CREED, with the date and the source. If it is not connected, say so and work from the pages. How to add it: https://advisor.apps.wayne.edu/llms.txt

Task:
1. Say which kind of app this is: raw PHP, raw PHP with Vue, Laravel with Blade, Laravel with Blade and Vue, or Laravel with Inertia and Vue.
2. List every version it declares or locks: the PHP floor, Laravel, Node, Vue, Inertia, and MySQL if you can tell.
3. For each one, give the state CREED assigns it today (Active, Security, Eol or EolGraceExpired), the date that state ends, and the clause that applies.
4. Propose the smallest change that moves anything past end of life onto a supported line. Do not make it yet.

Constraints:
- CREED decides a version's state. Never guess a date: read it from the policy or from ADVISOR, and say which.
- An app that reads the policy itself installs the reader with `composer require waynestate/creed`. Never copy policy.json into the app.
- Give separate commands for Windows (PowerShell), macOS and Linux wherever they differ.
- Ask me before you guess: a version you cannot read, an app kind you cannot tell, or anything that touches a deploy.

Output: a table (component, version, state, until, clause), then the change as numbered steps, then your questions.
```

#### Or start from your consumer path

#### CREED in a raw PHP app

Every rule that applies to an app with no framework, checked with the file and line as evidence.

A prompt for your coding agent. Copy it as it stands:

```text
You are a coding agent reviewing a raw PHP app (no framework) at Wayne State University against CREED, the written standard of WELD, the Wayne State application stack.

Read first:
- https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/llms.txt, then the handbook chapters it lists. Every rule there cites the decision behind it.
- ADVISOR, the stack's MCP server, if it is connected: call list_stack_rules with permutation raw-php (raw-php-vue if the app builds Vue), and policy_lookup for each runtime. If it is not connected, say so and work from the handbook pages.
- composer.json, composer.lock, the entry scripts or front controller, and any CI file.

Task:
1. Check the app against the rules that apply to raw PHP: versions, dependencies, secrets and configuration, runtime and headers, auth, and CI.
2. For each rule, record Pass, Fail or Cannot tell, with the file and line that shows it.
3. Change nothing yet. Propose the three fixes that buy the most, smallest first.

Constraints:
- Cite the chapter and rule for every finding: the handbook file and line from ADVISOR, or the page URL.
- A raw PHP app has no framework to lean on. Say what the app itself must do, and never suggest adding Laravel just to meet a rule.
- The PHP floor comes from the policy, not from memory.
- Ask me before you guess, and before you touch anything that deploys.

Output: a findings table (rule, chapter, result, evidence), then the three fixes, then your questions.
```

#### CREED in a Laravel app with Blade

The same inspection, the Laravel way: config, middleware and the framework line from the policy.

A prompt for your coding agent. Copy it as it stands:

```text
You are a coding agent reviewing a Laravel app that renders its pages with Blade, at Wayne State University, against CREED, the written standard of WELD, the Wayne State application stack.

Read first:
- https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/llms.txt, then the handbook chapters it lists. Every rule there cites the decision behind it.
- ADVISOR, the stack's MCP server, if it is connected: call list_stack_rules with permutation laravel-blade (laravel-blade-vue if Blade pages mount Vue components), and policy_lookup for PHP and Laravel. If it is not connected, say so and work from the handbook pages.
- composer.json, composer.lock, config/, bootstrap/app.php, .env.example, and any CI file.

Task:
1. Check the app against the rules that apply to Laravel with Blade: the PHP floor and the Laravel line, dependencies, secrets and .env, runtime and headers, auth, and CI.
2. For each rule, record Pass, Fail or Cannot tell, with the file and line that shows it.
3. Change nothing yet. Propose the three fixes that buy the most, smallest first.

Constraints:
- Cite the chapter and rule for every finding: the handbook file and line from ADVISOR, or the page URL.
- Meet a rule the Laravel way (config, middleware, a service provider) before writing code of your own.
- Laravel's support dates come from CREED's policy, not from memory or from laravel.com.
- Ask me before you guess, and before you touch migrations or anything that deploys.

Output: a findings table (rule, chapter, result, evidence), then the three fixes, then your questions.
```

#### CREED in a Laravel app with Inertia and Vue

Both halves inspected: the Composer side and the npm side, Node, Vue and Inertia included.

A prompt for your coding agent. Copy it as it stands:

```text
You are a coding agent reviewing a Laravel app with Inertia and Vue, at Wayne State University, against CREED, the written standard of WELD, the Wayne State application stack. It has two halves, and CREED covers both.

Read first:
- https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/llms.txt, then the handbook chapters it lists. Every rule there cites the decision behind it.
- ADVISOR, the stack's MCP server, if it is connected: call list_stack_rules with permutation laravel-inertia-vue, and policy_lookup for PHP, Laravel, Node, Vue and Inertia. If it is not connected, say so and work from the handbook pages.
- The PHP half: composer.json, composer.lock, config/, .env.example. The frontend half: package.json, its lock file, .npmrc, the Vite config. And any CI file.

Task:
1. Check the app against the rules that apply to Laravel with Inertia and Vue: the PHP, Laravel, Node, Vue and Inertia lines, dependencies on both sides, secrets and .env, runtime and headers, auth, and CI.
2. For each rule, record Pass, Fail or Cannot tell, with the file and line that shows it.
3. Change nothing yet. Propose the three fixes that buy the most, smallest first.

Constraints:
- Cite the chapter and rule for every finding: the handbook file and line from ADVISOR, or the page URL.
- The npm side counts as much as the Composer side: a missing or uncommitted lock file is a finding.
- Every support date comes from CREED's policy, never from memory.
- Ask me before you guess, and before you touch migrations, the build, or anything that deploys.

Output: a findings table (rule, chapter, result, evidence, half), then the three fixes, then your questions.
```

The agent reads the same pages you do: [llms.txt](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/llms.txt) lists them, [llms-full.txt](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/llms-full.txt) holds them all in one file, and every page has a Markdown twin. Nothing here phones home; the buttons only copy text or open the tool you picked. The inspector never guesses, and neither should the agent.

Chapter 9

## Accessibility

1 provision

To be decided

Key words The key words **MUST**, **MUST NOT**, **SHOULD**, **SHOULD NOT** and **MAY** in this chapter are to be interpreted as described in [RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119).

To be decided. No ADR decides the accessibility rules yet, so this chapter states no rules.

What is known:

- [WayneUI](https://wayneui.apps.wayne.edu/) is the component library the stack builds on.

When the accessibility rules are decided, they will land here, with the ADR number that decided them.

Chapter 4

## Auth

6 provisions

Partly decided

Key words The key words **MUST**, **MUST NOT**, **SHOULD**, **SHOULD NOT** and **MAY** in this chapter are to be interpreted as described in [RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119).

- One protocol-neutral library, named for what it does, not how. It returns a verified identity and leaves the session to the app (the stack's auth design).
- The app always owns its session. Every driver ends in the app's `findOrImportUser(identity)`, and the protocol never holds the session (the stack's auth design).
- The `gateway` driver accepts only a signed assertion, never a bare header: user, attributes, issued-at, audience, an expiry of 60 seconds or less, and a signature the gateway and app share (the stack's auth design).
- Drivers: `cas` (the default today), `gateway`, `oidc`, `oauth2`, `saml` (not built yet), and `fake` for local development and tests (the stack's auth design).
- Non-EOL PHP only, with no exceptions (the stack's auth design).
- To be decided: the gateway's key distribution and rotation, and the SAML library choice if a `saml` driver is built (the stack's auth design).

Set from [`handbook/auth.md` on GitHub](https://github.com/waynestate/creed/blob/main/handbook/auth.md), impression `bf348fb`. Found a mistake? Fix the Markdown; this page is rebuilt from it.

---

Source: https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/ci.html

Chapter 8

## CI

5 provisions · **MUST** 1

Decided

Key words The key words **MUST**, **MUST NOT**, **SHOULD**, **SHOULD NOT** and **MAY** in this chapter are to be interpreted as described in [RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119).

- CI is enforcement point (c): a red pipeline before merge (the stack's enforcement design).
- The CI components are [Preflight](https://preflight.apps.wayne.edu/)'s: `proctor`, `php-test` and `composer-audit`, included with `include: component:` (first-repos).
- CI judges with deterministic commands, never with a model. No gate depends on a model's opinion (the stack's rule on language models).
- Components are pinned at a tag or SHA, never `~latest` (first-repos).
- git.wayne.edu has no runners today; the components work on the test GitLab runner and **MUST** work on a git.wayne.edu runner when one exists (first-repos). Every product strongly recommends the instance runner.

Set from [`handbook/ci.md` on GitHub](https://github.com/waynestate/creed/blob/main/handbook/ci.md), impression `c7f3b98`. Found a mistake? Fix the Markdown; this page is rebuilt from it.

---

Source: https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/code.html

Chapter 3

## Code

10 sections · 33 provisions · **MUST NOT** 1

Partly decided

Key words The key words **MUST**, **MUST NOT**, **SHOULD**, **SHOULD NOT** and **MAY** in this chapter are to be interpreted as described in [RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119).

### [§3.1](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/code.html#php-style) PHP style

- Laravel apps use Pint's `laravel` preset (the stack's coding standard).
- Raw PHP apps and the stack's own packages use the `per` preset, PER Coding Style 3.1 (the stack's coding standard).
- One formatter per repo, never two (the stack's coding standard).
- An app points Pint at the preset in `vendor/waynestate/pinstripe/pint/` with `--config` (the stack's coding standard).
- Files are UTF-8 without a BOM, with LF line endings (the stack's every-OS design).

### [§3.2](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/code.html#static-analysis) Static analysis

- PHPStan level 8 for new code: the stack's own packages and every app [Sourdough](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/) generates (the stack's coding standard).
- Larastan loads only where Laravel is present (the stack's coding standard).
- Every inline ignore carries an identifier and a reason; configs set `reportIgnoresWithoutComments` (the stack's coding standard).
- PHPStan's `phpVersion` follows the policy's PHP floor (the stack's coding standard).
- Existing apps start at the highest level they pass, with a committed baseline that **MUST NOT** grow, then raise the level one step at a time (the stack's coding standard). Like the band says, the only way is Higher.
- New packages have no baseline (the stack's coding standard).
- Two reasons for level 8:
  - The starters begin clean, so new apps pass from day one (the stack's coding standard).
  - Null handling is the class of bug level 8 adds; in the stack's auth and header code, a null bug is a security bug (the stack's coding standard).

### [§3.3](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/code.html#banned-patterns) Banned patterns

Each ban becomes a PHPStan rule: Larastan's where it has one, `phpstan-disallowed-calls` for plain bans, and a custom rule only when neither fits.

- `env()` only in `config/` files, from Larastan's `NoEnvCallsOutsideOfConfig` rule. Planned.
- No disabled TLS verification, such as `withoutVerifying()` or `CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER` set to false (OWASP ASVS). Planned.
- No SQL built by joining strings; use bindings (OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet). Planned.
- No debug leftovers or dynamic code, from `phpstan-disallowed-calls`. Planned.

### [§3.4](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/code.html#vue-and-javascript) Vue and JavaScript

- ESLint flat config (the stack's coding standard).
- `eslint-plugin-vue` `flat/recommended` (the stack's coding standard).
- Prettier for formatting (the stack's coding standard).
- `eslint-plugin-vuejs-accessibility` (the stack's coding standard).
- Both JavaScript and TypeScript are linted (the stack's coding standard).
- The stack's Vue starters use TypeScript; plain JavaScript stays fully supported (the stack's coding standard).
- Node 22.13 or newer for the lint tools (the stack's coding standard).

### [§3.5](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/code.html#security-analysis) Security analysis

- The stack's GitLab instances run the Free tier, so nothing relies on GitLab SAST (the stack's coding standard).
- The open tools instead: Larastan's env rule, `phpstan-disallowed-calls`, and a Psalm taint-analysis pilot on one app (the stack's coding standard).

### [§3.6](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/code.html#how-it-is-enforced) How it is enforced

- Pint, PHPStan, Rector dry-runs and ESLint run in CI through [Preflight](https://preflight.apps.wayne.edu/) components, not in the deploy gate (the stack's coding standard). The Preflight components are Planned.
- New rules arrive as warnings and become errors on a stated date, the same staging as PHP versions (the stack's enforcement design).
- [PROCTOR](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/) reports whether an app uses the presets (the stack's coding standard). The PROCTOR report is Planned.

### [§3.7](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/code.html#which-preset-enforces-each-rule) Which preset enforces each rule

Table 3-1

| Rule | Preset file | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PHP style, Laravel apps | `pint/laravel.json` | Planned |
| PHP style, raw PHP apps and stack packages | `pint/per.json` | Planned |
| Static analysis, level 8 | `phpstan/base.neon` | Planned |
| Static analysis, raw apps | `phpstan/raw.neon` | Planned |
| Static analysis, Laravel apps | `phpstan/laravel.neon` | Planned |
| Banned patterns | to be decided (a [Pinstripe](https://pinstripe.apps.wayne.edu/) PHPStan config) | Planned |
| Vue and JavaScript | the ESLint package (name to be decided) | Planned |
| Security analysis | to be decided | Planned |

### [§3.8](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/code.html#not-adopted) Not adopted

- Mago and PHP_CodeSniffer 4 are not adopted; Pint is the only formatter (the stack's coding standard).
- Mago is looked at again before Pinstripe 1.0 (the stack's coding standard).

### [§3.9](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/code.html#to-be-decided) To be decided

- `declare(strict_types=1)` in every file. The sources recommend it, but the stack's coding standard does not decide it.
- `phpstan-strict-rules` for the stack's packages (the stack's coding standard).
- Where the ESLint package is published (the stack's coding standard).

### [§3.10](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/code.html#sources) Sources

- PER Coding Style 3.1: [https://www.php-fig.org/per/coding-style/](https://www.php-fig.org/per/coding-style/)
- PSR-1 Basic Coding Standard: [https://www.php-fig.org/psr/psr-1/](https://www.php-fig.org/psr/psr-1/)
- Laravel Pint, 13.x docs: [https://laravel.com/docs/13.x/pint](https://laravel.com/docs/13.x/pint)
- PHPStan, rule levels: [https://phpstan.org/user-guide/rule-levels](https://phpstan.org/user-guide/rule-levels)
- PHPStan, baseline: [https://phpstan.org/user-guide/baseline](https://phpstan.org/user-guide/baseline)
- PHPStan, configuration reference: [https://phpstan.org/config-reference](https://phpstan.org/config-reference)
- PHPStan, ignoring errors: [https://phpstan.org/user-guide/ignoring-errors](https://phpstan.org/user-guide/ignoring-errors)
- Larastan: [https://github.com/larastan/larastan](https://github.com/larastan/larastan)

- spaze/phpstan-disallowed-calls: [https://github.com/spaze/phpstan-disallowed-calls](https://github.com/spaze/phpstan-disallowed-calls)

- eslint-plugin-vuejs-accessibility docs: [https://vue-a11y.github.io/eslint-plugin-vuejs-accessibility/](https://vue-a11y.github.io/eslint-plugin-vuejs-accessibility/)
- Node.js release schedule: [https://github.com/nodejs/Release](https://github.com/nodejs/Release)
- Psalm, security analysis: [https://psalm.dev/docs/security_analysis/](https://psalm.dev/docs/security_analysis/)
- GitLab SAST: [https://docs.gitlab.com/user/application_security/sast/](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/application_security/sast/)
- OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet: [https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/SQL_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/SQL_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html)
- GitLab Code Quality: [https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/testing/code_quality/](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/testing/code_quality/)
- OWASP ASVS: [https://asvs.owasp.org/](https://asvs.owasp.org/)

Chapter 5

## Databases

7 sections · 23 provisions · **MAY** 1

Decided

Key words The key words **MUST**, **MUST NOT**, **SHOULD**, **SHOULD NOT** and **MAY** in this chapter are to be interpreted as described in [RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119).

### [§5.1](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/databases.html#what-the-stack-supports) What the stack supports

The policy lists the MySQL versions in [`policy/policy.json`](https://github.com/waynestate/creed/blob/main/policy/policy.json), under `mysql`: 5.6, 5.7, 8.0, 8.4 and 9.7, each with its [`active_until`](https://github.com/waynestate/creed/blob/main/policy/policy.json) and [`security_until`](https://github.com/waynestate/creed/blob/main/policy/policy.json) dates. The shared server runs 5.6, which is past security support; its `security_until` is 2021-02-28. Laravel 13 documents MySQL 5.7 or later. The conventions below keep an app working on the shared server until it is upgraded. They are a bridge, not the fix: the fix is the upgrade. Code that follows them runs unchanged on 8.4, so the move can be made With Arms Wide Open.

### [§5.2](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/databases.html#grace-period) Grace period

An app **MAY** stay on a database version for 90 days after it leaves support, the policy's [`eol_grace_days`](https://github.com/waynestate/creed/blob/main/policy/policy.json); the version is `Eol` through that window and `EolGraceExpired` the day after, when the gate fails with no override. The window is a bridge for the upgrade, not a second support window: the fix is still the upgrade.

### [§5.3](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/databases.html#conventions-that-keep-5-6-working) Conventions that keep 5.6 working

- Set `Schema::defaultStringLength(191)` in `AppServiceProvider::boot()`, before any migration runs. 5.6 caps an indexed `utf8mb4` column at 767 bytes, which is 191 characters.
- Keep `utf8mb4` and `utf8mb4_unicode_ci`, the defaults. Never use an 8.0-only collation such as `utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci` (not yet confirmed on a 5.6 server).
- Store JSON as `text` or `longText`, with Eloquent `array` or `json` casts, and filter in PHP. 5.6 has no JSON column type.
- Leave `use_upsert_alias` unset, so `upsert()` uses `VALUES()`. The row alias that setting switches to needs MySQL 8.0.19.
- Rename a column with raw `DB::statement('ALTER TABLE ... CHANGE ...')`. Avoid `renameColumn` and `renameIndex`, which emit 5.7 syntax.
- Use `Schema::hasTable` only. Column introspection is not reliable on 5.6 (not yet confirmed on a 5.6 server).
- Skip `db:show` and `db:monitor`, and run one database-queue worker (or another driver if the platform offers one). 5.6 has no `SKIP LOCKED`, so a single worker avoids double-processing.
- Use `timestamp`, not `date`, for `useCurrent()`. A `date` column cannot take a current-timestamp default on 5.6.
- Run migrations in CI against a real 5.6 container. SQLite-only tests pass code that 5.6 rejects.

### [§5.4](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/databases.html#avoid-until-the-server-is-upgraded) Avoid until the server is upgraded

#### [§5.4.1](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/databases.html#schema) Schema

- JSON and jsonb columns
- Generated columns
- `renameIndex` and `renameColumn`
- Column introspection
- `invisible`, `instant` and `vector` columns
- InnoDB `spatialIndex` (needs 5.7.5, not yet confirmed on a 5.6 server)
- DESC indexes and CHECK constraints

#### [§5.4.2](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/databases.html#queries) Queries

- `whereJson*` and JSON-path updates
- Window functions and CTEs
- `SKIP LOCKED` and `NOWAIT` in raw SQL
- `joinLateral`
- Joined deletes with an order or a limit

#### [§5.4.3](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/databases.html#commands) Commands

- `db:show`
- `db:monitor`

### [§5.5](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/databases.html#moving-to-8-4) Moving to 8.4

Code that follows the conventions and avoids the patterns above runs unchanged on 8.4. The server-side large-prefix settings (`innodb_large_prefix=ON`, `innodb_file_format=Barracuda`, DYNAMIC rows) are a question for the database owners, not something an app sets (not yet confirmed on a 5.6 server). Passing `ROW_FORMAT=DYNAMIC` through the `engine` config is likewise not yet confirmed on a 5.6 server.

Oracle moved 5.6 to Sustaining Support on 2021-02-01, so it gets no new fixes. Builds older than 5.6.46 also speak only TLS 1.0, which current hosts may refuse (not yet confirmed on a 5.6 server). Both are reasons to plan the move rather than wait for it.

### [§5.6](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/databases.html#how-the-stack-checks-it) How the stack checks it

[PROCTOR](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/) will flag the patterns in the avoid list above. Not yet.

### [§5.7](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/databases.html#sources) Sources

- Laravel 13 database docs: [https://laravel.com/docs/13.x/database](https://laravel.com/docs/13.x/database)

Chapter 2

## Dependencies

1 section · 13 provisions · **MUST NOT** 4 · **MUST** 6 · **SHOULD NOT** 1 · **SHOULD** 1

Decided

Key words The key words **MUST**, **MUST NOT**, **SHOULD**, **SHOULD NOT** and **MAY** in this chapter are to be interpreted as described in [RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119).

- No `dev-master`, `dev-*` or `*` constraints on runtime dependencies (the stack's version policy).
- A lock file is required and **MUST** be committed (the stack's version policy).
- `composer audit` **MUST** report no advisories at or above the policy's severity threshold (the stack's version policy).
- `composer.json` `require.php` **MUST NOT** allow an EOL version as its lowest bound (the stack's version policy).
- Every project is a framework-free core plus thin adapters. `composer.json` requires only `php` and PSR packages; Laravel, Inertia and Vue are `suggest` (the stack's core-plus-adapters design).
- Adapters call the core and never re-implement it (the stack's core-plus-adapters design).

### [§2.1](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/dependencies.html#private-packages) Private packages

- Internal-only packages **MUST** be installed from one GitLab package registry per ecosystem (Composer, npm), not from one `vcs`, `path` or `artifact` repository entry per package (the stack's private-packages decision).
- Credentials **MUST NOT** appear in any repository URL in `composer.json` or `composer.lock`, or as a literal value in a committed `.npmrc`. Tokens live in a gitignored `auth.json`, the npm user config, or a CI or build-time secret (the stack's private-packages decision).
- Builds **MUST** use a read-only deploy token (`read_package_registry` only); personal access tokens **MUST NOT** be used in builds (the stack's private-packages decision).
- The private Composer registry entry **MUST** be canonical, and the Packagist entry **SHOULD** exclude the internal vendor names, so a public package with the same name can never be installed instead (the stack's private-packages decision).
- A released version **MUST** map to one commit for ever: tags are protected, and a version is never republished from a different commit (the stack's private-packages decision).
- Public code **MUST NOT** go through the private registry; it is published to Packagist or npm (the stack's private-packages decision).
- Apps **SHOULD NOT** proxy or mirror public registries in v1 (the stack's private-packages decision).

[PROCTOR](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/)'s `repo-url-credentials`, `package-sources` and `internal-vendor-shadowing` checks enforce rules 1, 2 and 4 (warning first), and [Preflight](https://preflight.apps.wayne.edu/)'s publish job enforces rule 5.

Set from [`handbook/dependencies.md` on GitHub](https://github.com/waynestate/creed/blob/main/handbook/dependencies.md), impression `40008d6`. Found a mistake? Fix the Markdown; this page is rebuilt from it.

Source: https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/deploy-gate.html

Chapter 7

## Deploy gate

2 sections · 8 provisions

Decided

Key words The key words **MUST**, **MUST NOT**, **SHOULD**, **SHOULD NOT** and **MAY** in this chapter are to be interpreted as described in [RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119).

The deploy gate runs [PROCTOR](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/) against the commit being released, before it is released, and refuses EOL PHP (the stack's deploy-gate decision).

- The deploy-time rule set is small, offline and fast: the target image's status and its PHP version against [`policy.json`](https://github.com/waynestate/creed/blob/main/policy/policy.json), the framework and stack package versions in `composer.lock`, and known advisories from a cached database (the stack's deploy-gate decision).
- EOL fails: a deploy that regresses a rule, a new app that fails any rule, or an expired override is blocked (the stack's deploy-gate decision).
- It ratchets: a deploy that doesn't make things worse always passes (the stack's deploy-gate decision).
- Each rule moves through stages, `report`, `warn`, `block`, with dates in `policy.json` (the stack's deploy-gate decision).

### [§7.1](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/deploy-gate.html#on-citadel) On Citadel

- Citadel runs the gate in its release hook: `proctor gate` in `runGitPull()`, against the fetched commit, before it is checked out (the stack's deploy-gate decision).
- The gate is pending the Citadel team, which is still an open question. Until it is adopted, enforcement is CI on the test GitLab instance (the stack's deploy-gate decision).

### [§7.2](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/deploy-gate.html#elsewhere) Elsewhere

- The same gate runs as a CI job through [Preflight](https://preflight.apps.wayne.edu/)'s `proctor` component, wherever the pipeline runs (first-repos).
- [Squire](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/)'s `docker` target will run the gate before it ships an image, and so will its later `openshift` and `coolify` targets (the stack's rule that packages run on any container platform).

Set from [`handbook/deploy-gate.md` on GitHub](https://github.com/waynestate/creed/blob/main/handbook/deploy-gate.md), impression `a557384`. Found a mistake? Fix the Markdown; this page is rebuilt from it.

Source: https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/every-os.html

Chapter 10

## Every OS

5 provisions · **MUST** 1

Decided

Key words The key words **MUST**, **MUST NOT**, **SHOULD**, **SHOULD NOT** and **MAY** in this chapter are to be interpreted as described in [RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119).

- Every developer tool works on Windows, macOS and Linux (the stack's every-OS design).
- A developer script ships as a `.ps1` and `.sh` pair that do the same thing, or as one PHP command, which works the same everywhere (the stack's every-OS design).
- Windows gets PowerShell (`.ps1`), which never needs bash or WSL. Linux and macOS get bash (`.sh`), written for macOS's stock bash 3.2 and its BSD tools (the stack's every-OS design).
- Every repo carries a `.gitattributes` with `* text=auto eol=lf`, and `.ps1`, `.bat` and `.cmd` set to CRLF. Anything that runs on a Linux host **MUST** be LF: on Citadel, and on OpenShift, Coolify or raw Docker elsewhere (the stack's every-OS design).
- Paths are built with the language's path functions, and subprocesses start with argument arrays, never shell strings (the stack's every-OS design).

Set from [`handbook/every-os.md` on GitHub](https://github.com/waynestate/creed/blob/main/handbook/every-os.md), impression `a82b107`. Found a mistake? Fix the Markdown; this page is rebuilt from it.

### How to read this book

- **[§3.2](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/#contents)**: Chapter 3, section 2. Every section number is a link to itself: copy it to cite the rule.
- ****MUST** **SHOULD** **MAY****: The RFC 2119 key words, set in small capitals so a requirement never hides in a sentence.
- **(the stack's version policy)**: The decision a rule comes from. Rules state what is decided and cite it.
- **Not yet**: "To be decided": the gap is printed, and no rule is stated in its place.

[The whole book on one page](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/print.html)

For printing, or for your browser's find. Every chapter, in order, from the same Markdown.

Chapter 11

## Overrides

5 provisions

Decided

Key words The key words **MUST**, **MUST NOT**, **SHOULD**, **SHOULD NOT** and **MAY** in this chapter are to be interpreted as described in [RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119).

- Overrides are named, dated and visible (the stack's version policy).
- An app keeps a `policy-overrides.json` with an expiry date and a reason (the stack's version policy).
- Check prints every override on every run, and Fleet lists them (the stack's version policy).
- An expired override is a failure (first-repos).
- On the Citadel side, overrides are held by Citadel admins, per app and per rule, with an expiry, a reason and an approver. There is no permanent override (the stack's deploy-gate decision).

Chapter 1

## Versions

2 sections · 4 provisions · **MUST** 1

Decided

Key words The key words **MUST**, **MUST NOT**, **SHOULD**, **SHOULD NOT** and **MAY** in this chapter are to be interpreted as described in [RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119).

The stack's version policy states:

Table 1-1

| State | Runtime (Baseline) | Check / CI | Platform |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| active | silent | pass |  |
| security-only | ribbon warning in non-production; log line in production | warning |  |
| EOL | ribbon error in non-production; daily log line | fail | Citadel retires the image on its own schedule; elsewhere the owner retires it, and the gate fails either way |
| EOL + 90 days | as above | fail; no override |  |

- The dates live in [`policy/policy.json`](https://github.com/waynestate/creed/blob/main/policy/policy.json). Every tool derives a version's state from the date, through the CREED reader. No other code decides state (the stack's version policy).
- The PHP floor is `^8.2`, the oldest non-EOL version today (the stack's version policy). It moves to `^8.3` on 2027-01-01.
- Stack packages raise their own `php` floor in a new major when a PHP version reaches EOL, so security fixes require the upgrade (the stack's version policy).
- `policy.json` is a contract, versioned like [WayneUI](https://wayneui.apps.wayne.edu/)'s `/v2/`. Older Check versions **MUST** still read newer policy files (the stack's version policy).

### [§1.1](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/versions.html#latest-patches) Latest patches

Each version can also carry a [`latest_patch`](https://github.com/waynestate/creed/blob/main/policy/policy.json): the newest patch release for that version as of a [`latest_patch_checked`](https://github.com/waynestate/creed/blob/main/policy/policy.json) date. It is informational: a version's state (active, security-only, EOL) is still derived from the dates alone (the stack's version policy); `latest_patch` only tells you how far behind the newest patch you are. `bin/refresh-patches.php` keeps it current by reading the four upstream feeds (php.net's active releases, Packagist's `laravel/framework`, nodejs.org's dist index, and endoflife.date's PHP data) and writing `latest_patch` and `latest_patch_checked` for every version the feeds cover; a version the feeds do not cover (an EOL branch, for instance) is left as-is with a warning, and a php.net / endoflife.date disagreement is reported but never fails the run. Run it with `--dry-run` to preview, or `--offline <dir>` to test against saved feeds.

### [§1.2](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/versions.html#tool-minimums) Tool minimums

The `tools` block sets a minimum version for a developer tool. Each key is a tool name, each value a `minimum` version. Today it holds Composer at 2.8.0.

Composer 2.8.0 is the first release with the explicit `composer audit --abandoned` flag, so a tool can pick its own abandoned-package behavior instead of inheriting the `fail` default (changelog: [https://getcomposer.org/changelog/2.8.0](https://getcomposer.org/changelog/2.8.0)).

[PROCTOR](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/) will check a developer's Composer against this minimum and fail fast below it. The minimum is a floor, not a ceiling: we do not go lower, no matter how the crowd sings for more.

In [`policy.json`](https://github.com/waynestate/creed/blob/main/policy/policy.json)

- **`components.*.versions.*.latest_patch`**: set per version
- **`components.*.versions.*.latest_patch_checked`**: set per version

Set from [`handbook/versions.md` on GitHub](https://github.com/waynestate/creed/blob/main/handbook/versions.md), impression `3e6f4bc`. Found a mistake? Fix the Markdown; this page is rebuilt from it.
